Materials

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
The field of Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (FSCIL) faces a critical bottleneck: the "stability-plasticity" dilemma is exacerbated when data is scarce. While prompt-based methods have successfully mitigated catastrophic forgetting in standard continual learning, they rely heavily on abundant data to tune prompts. In few-shot scenarios, these methods struggle to capture robust class representations, leading to overfitting on new tasks and interference with previously learned classes. A fundamental limitation is that current prompting strategies treat all features uniformly; they do not explicitly distinguish between **discriminative features** (critical for classification) and **non-discriminative features** (background noise or commonalities), resulting in "noisy" prompts that hinder precise boundary formation between classes.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can stabilize few-shot incremental learning by mimicking the human cognitive process of "selective attention." We posit that explicitly decomposing the prompt learning process into two semantic streams—**Discriminative** (class-specific) and **Non-Discriminative** (task-agnostic)—will allow the model to isolate essential class patterns while safely accounting for irrelevant variations. By treating non-discriminative information not as mere noise to be discarded, but as a separate semantic component to be modeled, we believe we can enhance the separation of class distributions and prevent the "over-memorization" of sparse samples.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a framework named **Semantic Complementary Prompting (SEC-Prompt)**. The approach treats the pre-trained backbone as frozen and injects learnable parameters via a dual-stream strategy.

1.  **Adaptive Hierarchical Querying:**
    Instead of relying on a static feature vector from the final layer of the backbone (which limits adaptation), we will implement an adaptive query mechanism. We will extract query tokens from the input of various transformer layers. This allows the prompting mechanism to access and leverage hierarchical feature abstractions—ranging from low-level textures to high-level semantic concepts—dynamically adjusting to the evolving feature space.

2.  **Discriminative Prompt (D-Prompt) Stream:**
    We will design a prompt module focused solely on class separation.
    *   **Matching Mechanism:** This module will utilize a standard attention mechanism to match queries with keys in the prompt pool. It will amplify features that highly correlate with specific classes.
    *   **Clustering Regulation:** To prevent these prompts from overfitting to outliers, we will employ a clustering objective that minimizes the distance between D-Prompts belonging to the same class, ensuring a compact and robust representation of class identity.

3.  **Non-Discriminative Prompt (ND-Prompt) Stream:**
    We will design a parallel module to capture task-agnostic information (e.g., background, style).
    *   **Reverse Attention:** Unlike standard prompting, this module will employ a *reverse* attention mechanism. It will assign higher weights to queries and keys that are *dissimilar*. By focusing on the "mismatches," the model learns to represent the dense, non-specific features that are shared across instances but irrelevant for classification.

4.  **ND-Based Data Augmentation:**
    To directly address the data scarcity in the few-shot setting, we will utilize the learned ND-Prompts. By injecting perturbations into the non-discriminative components of a sample, we can generate diverse synthetic training examples. This artificially expands the training set with variations in "style" or "background" while preserving the core "content" (discriminative features), thereby improving generalization.

## Expected Contribution
This research aims to establish a new paradigm for prompt engineering in continual learning by demonstrating the value of decoupled semantic modeling. Theoretically, it will validate that explicitly modeling non-discriminative features acts as a crucial regularizer for discriminative learning. Practically, we expect to deliver a parameter-efficient framework that significantly outperforms existing methods in minimizing catastrophic forgetting and overfitting, specifically within the challenging constraints of few-shot data streams.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a comprehensive evaluation framework to test the proposed SEC-Prompt method for Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (FSCIL).

*   **Datasets and Protocol:**
    *   **CIFAR100:** Organized into 60 base classes and 40 incremental classes. Structured as a 5-way 5-shot FSCIL scenario over 8 incremental sessions (9 sessions total).
    *   **CUB200-2011:** Organized into 100 base classes and 100 incremental classes. Structured as 10 incremental tasks (10-way 5-shot) over 11 sessions total.
    *   **ImageNet-R:** Organized into 100 base classes and 100 incremental classes. Structured as 10 incremental tasks (10-way 5-shot) over 11 sessions total.
    *   **Disjoint Sets:** Label sets were disjoint among sessions; test sets were cumulative (evaluating all seen classes).

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Top-1 Accuracy ($A_i$):** Measured after each session $i$.
    *   **Performance Dropping Rate (PD):** $A_0 - A_T$, measuring the drop between the base session and the final session.
    *   **Harmonic Accuracy (HAcc):** Evaluates balanced performance between base ($A_{base}$) and new ($A_{new}$) classes after the final task. Formula: $A_h = \frac{2 \times A_{base} \times A_{new}}{A_{base} + A_{new}}$.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Prompt-based CIL:** L2P, DualP, Coda-P.
    *   **FSCIL Algorithms:** TEEN, PriViLege, ASP.
    *   **Internal Baseline:** "Ours-F" (SEC-Prompt where no additional trainable parameters are introduced during incremental sessions).

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Backbone:** ViT-B/16-1K (pre-trained on ImageNet1K), fixed/frozen during training.
    *   **Input Resolution:** $224 \times 224$ for all datasets.
    *   **Prompt Length:** Set to 5 for ImageNet-R; Set to 3 for CIFAR100 and CUB200.
    *   **Prompt Pool Size:** Set to half the number of classes (e.g., 100 for ImageNet-R). We assigned one D-Prompt and one ND-Prompt component for every pair of classes.
    *   **Training Schedule (Base Session):** 30 epochs. SGD optimizer. Learning rate 0.1. Batch size: 64 (ImageNet-R), 32 (CIFAR100/CUB200).
    *   **Training Schedule (Incremental Sessions):** 10 epochs. Batch size 16. Learning rate: 0.0005 (ImageNet-R), 0.001 (CIFAR100/CUB200).
    *   **Hyperparameters:** $\lambda$ (Prompt Cluster Loss coefficient) = 0.5; $n$ (Augmentation perturbation groups) = 2.
    *   **Prompt Insertion Layers:** D-Prompt inserted at Layer 8; ND-Prompt inserted at Layer 5.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Overall Performance:** We observed that SEC-Prompt consistently outperformed other prompt-based and non-prompt-based methods in every incremental task (excluding the base session in some comparisons where full fine-tuning methods like TEEN performed higher).
*   **Metric Superiority:** On ImageNet-R, our method surpassed the state-of-the-art ASP method by 5.2% in Performance Dropping rate (PD) and 7.2% in Harmonic Accuracy (HAcc).
*   **Generalization (Ours-F):** The "Ours-F" variant (no training in incremental sessions) achieved the second-best performance among all methods, confirming strong generalization from the base session.
*   **Query Mechanism Analysis:** We found that the Adaptive Hierarchical Query (AHQ) mechanism significantly improved new class accuracy compared to a Fixed Query (FQ) approach. This held true for both the standard training and the frozen (-F) scenarios.
*   **Embedding Visualization (t-SNE):**
    *   Visualizations of feature embeddings showed that adding ND-Prompt significantly reduced the intra-class distance for base classes compared to using D-Prompt alone.
    *   Clusters for the SEC-Prompt method appeared more compact and centered.
    *   Even though ND-Prompt was not updated during incremental sessions, the intra-class features of novel classes (e.g., class 110) also became more compact in the SEC-Prompt visualization.
*   **Sensitivity Analysis ($\lambda$ and $n$):**
    *   We analyzed the coefficient for Discriminative Prompt Clustering Loss ($\lambda$) and found that $\lambda = 0.5$ yielded the highest accuracy in the last session across all three datasets.
    *   We analyzed the number of augmented sample groups ($n$) and found that $n=2$ provided optimal performance across all datasets.
*   **Hyperparameter Selection:**
    *   **Layer Depth:** We observed that D-Prompt accuracy peaked when inserted at Layer 8, while ND-Prompt accuracy peaked when inserted at Layer 5. This supports the hypothesis that D-Prompt captures high-level discriminative features (deeper) and ND-Prompt captures low-level non-discriminative features (shallower).
    *   **Prompt Length:** Performance improved with prompt length up to a length of 5, after which it plateaued or declined.
    *   **Prompt Pool Size:** Accuracy peaked at a pool size of 100 (for ImageNet-R), after which performance declined, suggesting larger pool sizes may induce greater forgetting.
*   **Parameter Efficiency:** Our method demonstrated higher performance with fewer trainable parameters compared to ASP and PriViLege. Specifically on CIFAR100 and CUB200, the parameter gap between our method and SOTA was narrower, aligning with the reduced difference in base class accuracy on these datasets compared to ImageNet-R.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The deployment of AI models in dynamic environments necessitates the capability of **Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (FSCIL)**. Models must integrate new classes from continuous data streams using only a limited number of examples while preserving performance on previously learned classes.

The central technical challenge is the **plasticity-stability dilemma**. While recent prompt-based Continual Learning (CIL) methods—such as L2P or Coda-Prompt—mitigate catastrophic forgetting by maintaining a pool of learnable prompts, they are fundamentally ill-equipped for the few-shot regime. These methods typically employ a key-query mechanism to retrieve prompts that maximize discriminative feature matching. However, they fail to distinguish between **discriminative features** (class-specific attributes) and **non-discriminative features** (task-agnostic information, background, style).

In few-shot scenarios, failing to decouple these feature types leads to severe overfitting. The model memorizes noise or non-discriminative patterns as class identities. Furthermore, existing methods utilize static queries derived from the frozen backbone's final output, which ignores the hierarchical evolution of feature abstraction across layers. We identify this inability to selectively attend to discriminative signals while robustly modeling non-discriminative context as the primary bottleneck in current FSCIL architectures.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose a novel framework titled **SEmantic Complementary Prompting (SEC-Prompt)**. Our core hypothesis is that by explicitly decoupling the prompt learning process into two complementary streams—**Discriminative Prompts (D-Prompt)** and **Non-Discriminative Prompts (ND-Prompt)**—we can simultaneously enhance class separation and generalization.

We hypothesize that:
1.  **D-Prompts** can be trained via a standard attention mechanism to isolate and strengthen class-specific features.
2.  **ND-Prompts** can be trained via a **Reverse Attention mechanism** to capture and balance task-agnostic information (mismatches), thereby reducing intra-class distances and preventing the model from overfitting to background noise.
3.  An **Adaptive Hierarchical Query** mechanism, deriving queries from layer-wise inputs rather than static final outputs, will allow the prompts to align dynamically with the evolving feature space of the Transformer.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will implement a Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) architecture where the Vision Transformer (ViT) backbone remains frozen. We will introduce learnable parameters (prompts) that are prepended to the input tokens of selected Transformer layers.

### 1. Visual Prompt Tuning Formulation
For the $i$-th layer, let the input token sequence be $h_i \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times D}$. We introduce a prompt $p_i \in \mathbb{R}^{L_p \times D}$, where $L_p$ is the prompt length. The operation for the layer is defined as:
$$ f_{ProT}(p_i, h_i) = \text{Layer}_i([p_i; h_i]) $$
where $[\cdot ; \cdot]$ denotes concatenation along the sequence length dimension.

### 2. Adaptive Hierarchical Query
To address the limitation of static queries, we will implement an adaptive query function. Instead of using the final [class] token, we effectively use the [class] token from the input of the *current* layer to query the prompt pool for the subsequent layer. For the $(i+1)$-th layer, the query $q_{i+1}(x)$ is defined as:
$$ q_{i+1}(x) = \text{Layer}_i([p_i, h_i])_{[class]} $$
This ensures the query dynamically aligns with the feature abstraction level of the specific layer.

### 3. Semantic Complementary Prompting (SEC-Prompt)
We will design the prompt pool to contain sets of parameters: Prompts $P$, Keys $K$, and Attention parameters $A$. We split the retrieval mechanism into two distinct pathways.

#### A. Discriminative Prompt (D-Prompt)
The D-Prompt is designed to enhance class separation. We will use an attention mechanism to calculate the similarity between the query and the keys. We apply a **Softmax** operation to emphasize the most relevant (matching) discriminative features:
$$ \alpha_{D}^j = \frac{e^{\alpha_{D}^j}}{\sum_{k} e^{\alpha_{D}^k}} $$
where the raw similarity score is computed via cosine similarity $\gamma$:
$$ \text{score} = \gamma(q(x) \odot A_{D}^j, K_{D}^j) $$
Here, $\odot$ represents the element-wise product. These weights $\alpha_{D}^j$ are then used to compute the weighted sum of D-Prompts.

#### B. Non-Discriminative Prompt (ND-Prompt)
The ND-Prompt aims to model task-agnostic features (noise/style) to prevent them from interfering with classification. We will employ a **Reverse Attention mechanism**. We focus on dissimilar queries and keys (mismatches) and truncate negative weights using a **ReLU** function instead of Softmax:
$$ \alpha_{ND}^j = \max(0, -\gamma(q(x) \odot A_{ND}^j, K_{ND}^j)) $$
This mechanism assigns high weights to mismatched features, effectively capturing non-discriminative information that the D-Prompt ignores.

### 4. Discriminative Prompt Clustering Loss
To prevent the D-Prompt from overfitting to non-discriminative features (noise) in the few-shot samples, we will introduce a **Prompt Clustering Loss** ($\mathcal{L}_{PC}$). This loss minimizes the distance between D-Prompt representations for samples belonging to the same class $y$:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{PC}(x, y) = \frac{1}{2N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} (1 - \gamma(p_{D}(x_i), p_{D}(x_j))) \cdot \mathbb{I}(y_i = y_j) $$
where $p_D(x)$ is the resulting D-Prompt for input $x$, $N$ is the batch size, and $\mathbb{I}$ is the indicator function. This encourages the model to learn shared discriminative traits rather than instance-specific noise.

### 5. ND-Prompt-Based Data Augmentation
To further mitigate overfitting, we will leverage the learned ND-Prompts for semantic data augmentation. Since ND-Prompts encapsulate non-discriminative information, perturbing them should generate diverse sample variations without altering the class identity.
We will introduce a spherical Gaussian perturbation to the weighting scores $\alpha_{ND}$:
$$ \tilde{\alpha}_{ND} = \alpha_{ND} + \mathcal{N}(0, 1) $$
These perturbed weights generate variants of the ND-Prompt, increasing sample diversity in the feature space during the incremental learning phases.

### 6. Optimization Objective
The model will be optimized using a combination of the standard Cross-Entropy loss ($\mathcal{L}_{CE}$) and the proposed Prompt Clustering loss, weighted by hyperparameter $\lambda$:
$$ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{CE}(x, y) + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{PC}(x, y) $$
During incremental sessions, we will freeze the ND-Prompts (assuming base classes provide sufficient non-discriminative coverage) and only expand the D-Prompt pool to accommodate new classes.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Theoretical Novelty:** We introduce the concept of "Semantic Complementary Prompting," providing a framework that explicitly models the dichotomy between discriminative and non-discriminative features in prompt learning.
2.  **Architectural Innovation:** The proposal of **Reverse Attention** for prompts and **Adaptive Hierarchical Queries** represents a significant departure from standard key-query prompt mechanisms, offering a more granular control over feature selection.
3.  **Robustness in Data Scarcity:** By utilizing ND-Prompts for feature-level data augmentation and implementing Prompt Clustering Loss, we expect to significantly reduce overfitting and catastrophic forgetting in few-shot scenarios compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
